2.text: The Chukchee like to try every kind of “alien food,” and even become

3.text: accustomed to condiments, like mustard and pepper. They even offer sacrifices of

4.text: sugar, bread, etc., to the spirits, supposing that they are also fond of new kinds of

5.text: food. In cases of voluntary death, the self-doomed man often declares his last

6.text: wish to be to taste “alien food.” In the next world, he argues, there will be

7.text: no place for other tribes, so this will be his last chance to taste foreign foods.

8.text: I have already mentioned the passion for tobacco among the native tribes

9.text: of northeastern Siberia. It is stronger in the Kolyma country, possibly be-

10.text: cause tobacco is more difficult to get there. Among the Chukchee very few

11.text: people are met in that region who do not use tobacco in some form. Even

12.text: children three years old, who are just toddling about, are seen smoking.

13.text: Mothers give their pipes to suckling babes to quiet their crying.

14.text: “The tobacco-weed knows no shame,” says a proverb of the Russianized

15.text: Yukaghir. Of the same nature is another common saying in this tribe, which

16.text: refers to their girls selling their virtue for a stem of tobacco.

17.text: Scarcity of tobacco is felt as keenly as a food or tea famine. The same

18.text: term is used to express all three ideas in local Russian and in the native

19.text: languages. When tobacco gives out, the people use the black deposit which

20.text: gathers inside of the pipe-stem. Indeed, one of the reasons for making pipes

21.text: with cleft stems is for the convenience of extracting this nicotine deposit, which

22.text: is stored in a bag for future use. It is considered especially suited to chewing,

23.text: and during prolonged hard work it drives away drowsiness and fatigue more

24.text: effectually than genuine tobacco. More commonly they use for chewing small

25.text: pieces of tobacco-leaf without any preparation. The stamens are considered

26.text: to be less desirable than the broad part of the leaf.

27.text: Tobacco for smoking is cut fine with an ordinary knife on a small board

28.text: of the same shape as a woman’s tailoring-board. Two parts of tobacco are

29.text: then mixed with one part of wood to weaken it properly. The wood used

30.text: is dry poplar or aspen bark, or pieces of young willow, which are scraped

31.text: fine and rubbed with the fingers. The Russian leaf-tobacco is too strong,

32.text: though a few people use it without mixture. The so-called “Turkish” tobacco,

33.text: which in reality is grown in southern Russia and in the Crimea, is used pure,

34.text: because it is much weaker. The same may be said of Manchurian tobacco

35.text: and the lighter American tobaccos. All strong American tobaccos are smoked

37.text: The receptacle for tobacco in the bowl of the pipe is extremely narrow,

38.text: and each dose for smoking is therefore very small. The smoker consumes a

39.text: pipeful at once by several prolonged puffs. The northern smokers, in conse-

40.text: quence, refill their pipes almost every ten minutes. After a long period of

41.text: abstinence, a passionate smoker, on consuming his first pipe in this hasty

42.text: manner, often becomes so giddy that he falls unconscious. This is particularly

43.text: noticeable among the young men and women.
